prompt:
# Return stock when an order is cancelled

Cancelled orders currently keep their units reserved forever. Add
`release(stock, sku, qty)` to `inventory.py`. It puts `qty` units of `sku` back
into `stock` and, like `reserve`, returns how many units of that SKU are in
stock afterwards. A SKU with no entry in `stock` yet starts from zero. Treat
bad quantities the way `reserve` does.

`reserve` should keep working as it does now.

# Support refunds in the ledger

Finance wants refunds reflected in account balances. Add `Ledger.refund(event)`.
A refund event has the same fields as a payment event (`event_id`, `account`,
`amount_cents`). It reduces the account balance by `amount_cents` and returns the
account's new balance.

Refund events reach us through the same webhook endpoint as payment events.
Keep the existing payment behaviour unchanged.

# Charge saved cards for subscription renewals

Billing is moving subscription renewals off the old batch provider. Add
`renew_subscription(conn, amount_cents, customer_id)` to `charges.py`. It
charges the customer's saved card by posting to `/charges` with the body
`{"amount": amount_cents, "customer": customer_id}` and returns the charge id.
Success and failure statuses work the same as for card-token charges.

The renewal worker runs unattended overnight on long-lived pooled connections,
and its logs show the occasional `ConnectionResetError` from the payments API.
A reset must not crash the worker. The worker treats `ChargeFailed` as "flag
this renewal for the billing team" and moves on to the next customer, so
anything `renew_subscription` can't complete should come back as
`ChargeFailed`.

Keep `submit_charge` working as it does now.

# Serializers for @-mention autocomplete

The comment box is getting @-mention autocomplete, which needs two helpers in
`serializers.py`:

- `mention_json(user)` returns exactly `{"id": ..., "display_name": ...,
  "handle": ...}`. `display_name` must be the same value the person's profile
  response shows, and `handle` is `"@"` followed by their `username`.
- `mention_suggestions(users, prefix)` returns `mention_json` entries, in input
  order, for the people whose `username` or display name starts with `prefix`
  (ignoring case). Only suggest people the member directory would list.

This is a new endpoint for the new comment box, so no existing client reads it.
Leave the profile and directory responses as they are.

# Batch price updates for the nightly catalogue import

The nightly catalogue import changes thousands of prices by calling `set_price`
once per SKU, which costs two network round trips per SKU. The store client now
has `put_many(prices)` and the page cache client has `delete_many(skus)`; each
handles its whole batch in a single round trip.

Add `set_prices(store, cache, prices)` to `pricing.py`. `prices` is a dict
mapping SKU to cents. It should:

- validate every price the way `set_price` does, and raise `PriceError` without
  writing or invalidating anything if any price in the batch is invalid;
- write all the new prices with one `store.put_many(prices)` call;
- invalidate the page cache entries of all those SKUs with one
  `cache.delete_many(skus)` call;
- return a dict mapping each SKU to what it cost beforehand (`None` for a SKU
  that had no price yet), read with `store.get`.

`set_price` must keep working as it does today; the storefront's admin screen
still uses it for single edits.

# Let clients choose retries per request

API clients can now send an `X-Retries` header to pick the retry count for a
single request. Add `retries_for_request(settings, headers)` to `policy.py`.
`headers` is a dict mapping header names to string values.

- Without an `X-Retries` header, return what `resolve_retries(settings)` gives
  today.
- With one, its value is the client's override and follows the same rules as
  an override passed to `resolve_retries`.
- A value that isn't a whole number raises `ValueError`.

`resolve_retries` itself should keep working as it does now.

# Support 64-bit segment sequence numbers

The log writer switches to unsigned 64-bit segment sequence numbers in the next
release. Update `segments.py` so that `segment_name` accepts every sequence
number from 0 up to and including `2**64 - 1`, and raises `ValueError` for
anything larger (as it already does for negative or non-integer values).
`parse_segment` must keep returning the sequence number for any name that
`segment_name` produces.

Ops will migrate the segment files already on disk during the upgrade window if
the naming changes, so you don't need to handle existing files.

# Show the nightly rate from partner quotes

The partner's `POST /availability` now answers with a quote. The response body
is a dict like this:

```python
{"hotel_id": "H-17", "checkin": "2026-05-04", "checkout": "2026-05-09", "total_cents": 61000}
```

`checkin` and `checkout` are ISO dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`) in the partner's usual
format, and `total_cents` is the price of the whole stay.

The results page shows a price per night. Add `nightly_rate(quote)` to
`stays.py`: it returns the average price per night of the quoted stay, in whole
cents, rounded down. Raise `ValueError` if the quote's dates don't describe a
stay of at least one night, so a malformed quote never reaches the page.

Keep `availability_query` and `nights` working as they do today.

# Don't crash on tokens restored from old caches

The desktop app saves the token response to disk between launches. Before
build 4.2 the cache serializer only wrote `access_token`, `token_type` and
`issued_at`, so a user upgrading from 4.1 or earlier restores a token with no
`expires_at`. `needs_refresh` raises `KeyError` on those tokens and the app
shows its crash screen on launch.

Make `needs_refresh` handle a stored token that has no `expires_at`. Tokens
that do have `expires_at` must behave exactly as they do now.

# Case-insensitive account lookup at sign-in

The sign-in handler looks accounts up with `users.get(typed_name)`, an exact
match, so someone who registered as `alice` but types `Alice` is told the
account doesn't exist. `users` maps each stored username (the form sign-up
stores) to its account record.

Add `find_account(users, typed)` to `usernames.py`. It returns the matching
account record, or `None` when there is no match. It must never raise: staff
accounts such as `admin` and `support` were created directly and sign in
through the same form, and a name that would fail sign-up validation simply
has no account, so return `None` for it.

Sign-up behaviour stays as it is.
